name: Ear infection (otitis media)
definition: An ear infection is an infection, usually of the middle ear behind the eardrum, that is common in children and often settles without treatment.
overview: Ear infections are common, especially in children, and usually settle without intervention. In the middle ear, blocked or swollen eustachian tubes let fluid build up behind the eardrum, which can lead to infection. Both viruses and bacteria can be responsible. Typical signs are earache, a fever, difficulty hearing and fluid leaking from the ear. Many ear infections get better on their own within about 3 days, and complications are rare.
causes: Viral infection is often the cause, although bacteria can be responsible too.
The bacteria most often involved include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.
Blocked or swollen eustachian tubes let fluid build up behind the eardrum, where it can become infected.
Allergies, colds, sinus infections, teething, enlarged adenoids and tobacco smoke are listed as triggers.
riskFactors: A family history of ear infections
A recent ear infection or other illness
Exposure to secondhand tobacco smoke, described as a major cause of ear infections in children
Young age: one review found the condition is most often seen between 6 and 24 months
signs: Redness of the eardrum, a bulging eardrum or fluid behind it on looking into the ear
Discharge, fluid or bleeding from the ear, which can indicate a perforated eardrum
Fluid in the middle ear detected by pneumatic otoscopy
complications: Slight short-term hearing loss during and just after the infection, because of fluid in the ear
Fluid that stays in the middle ear for weeks, known as glue ear
Spread of infection to the mastoid bone behind the ear (mastoiditis) or, rarely, to the meninges
Chronic otitis media or an abscess, which are rare
diagnosis: A clinician usually looks into the ear with an otoscope, checking for redness, a bulging eardrum or fluid behind it. Finding fluid in the middle ear with pneumatic otoscopy is described as key to establishing the diagnosis. A hearing test may be suggested if there is a history of repeated infections.
treatment: Many cases get better on their own, and for mild cases a clinician may recommend watchful waiting or delayed antibiotic prescribing. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease discomfort. Antibiotics are not usually offered for middle ear infections, because they make little difference to symptoms. NICE guideline NG91 supports either no antibiotic or a back-up antibiotic prescription for most children with acute otitis media, with some exceptions. A GP or pharmacist may prescribe eardrops or tablets for some types of ear infection.
prevention: Recommended vaccines, such as the flu and pneumococcal vaccines, are the main prevention advice from the CDC. Pneumococcal bacteria can cause ear infections, and limiting exposure to tobacco smoke is described as a way to lower risk.
seekCare: The NHS advises contacting a GP or NHS 111 urgently if the person feels generally unwell, has a very high temperature, has swelling around the ear, has new hearing loss, or has vomiting or dizziness. A child under 12 months with earache in both ears is also on that list. Pus or discharge from the ear, or symptoms lasting more than 2 to 3 days, are reasons to arrange a GP appointment. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of an ear infection?
sections.body:
The main signs of an ear infection are earache, a fever, difficulty hearing and fluid leaking from the ear. The NHS describes ear infections as common, especially in children. Young children may tug or rub at the ear, seem irritable or stop eating well. Difficulty sleeping is also listed among the common signs in children.

Symptoms that last more than 2 to 3 days or get worse are among the signs the CDC lists as pointing to a middle ear infection. Discharge, fluid or bleeding from the ear can indicate a perforated eardrum. A sudden end to severe pain may also indicate a ruptured eardrum. The NHS says that ear infections often get better on their own within about 3 days.

sections.heading: What causes ear infections?
sections.body:
Many ear infections follow a viral infection, although bacteria can also be the cause. The bacteria most often involved include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. In the middle ear, blocked or swollen eustachian tubes let fluid build up behind the eardrum, and this fluid can become infected. MedlinePlus lists allergies, colds and sinus infections, teething, enlarged adenoids and tobacco smoke as triggers.

Risk factors include attending daycare, using a pacifier, not being breastfed, a family history of ear infections and a recent illness. Secondhand smoke is described as a major cause of ear infections in children. One review found the condition is most often seen between 6 and 24 months of age. Pneumococcal bacteria, which a vaccine protects against, are among the causes of ear infections.

sections.heading: How is an ear infection diagnosed?
sections.body:
A clinician usually looks into the ear with an otoscope. They check for redness, a bulging eardrum or fluid behind the eardrum. Finding fluid in the middle ear with pneumatic otoscopy is described as key to establishing the diagnosis.

A hearing test may be suggested if a child has a history of repeated infections. Discharge, fluid or bleeding from the ear can point to a perforated eardrum. Infection of the outer ear, known as swimmer's ear, is a different condition from a middle ear infection. NICE guidance says symptoms should be reassessed at any time if they worsen rapidly or significantly. That reassessment considers other diagnoses, signs of more serious illness and previous antibiotic use, which may lead to resistant organisms.

sections.heading: How is an ear infection treated?
sections.body:
Many cases get better on their own, so a clinician may recommend watchful waiting. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease discomfort. The NHS advises keeping cotton buds and fingers out of the ear, keeping water out of it and avoiding swimming until it clears. Decongestants and antihistamines are not recommended, because there is no evidence that they help.

Antibiotics are not usually offered for middle ear infections, because they make little difference to symptoms. NICE guideline NG91 supports either no antibiotic or a back-up antibiotic prescription for most children with acute otitis media. A back-up prescription can be used if symptoms significantly worsen or do not improve within 3 days. Immediate antibiotics are offered where a child is very unwell, has signs of a more serious illness or is at high risk of complications. They can also be considered for children under 2 years with infection in both ears, or for children of any age with fluid draining from the ear.

sections.heading: What complications can an ear infection cause?
sections.body:
Most children have slight short-term hearing loss during and just after an ear infection, because of fluid in the ear. If fluid stays in the middle ear for weeks after the infection, the condition is called glue ear. Glue ear is not itself an ear infection, and it usually affects children under 7, most often between 2 and 5. The hearing loss it causes is usually mild or moderate, and many cases clear without treatment.

One NHS leaflet says glue ear needs treating only if it causes persistent hearing loss, speech delay or recurrent ear infections. Grommets are very small plastic tubes placed in the eardrum that let air move in and out of the middle ear. Hearing aids are an alternative in some cases. MedlinePlus lists rarer complications as a torn eardrum, spread of infection to the mastoid bone behind the ear or to the meninges, chronic otitis media and abscess.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help?
sections.body:
The NHS advises contacting a GP or NHS 111 urgently if the person feels generally unwell, has a very high temperature, has swelling around the ear or has new hearing loss. Vomiting or dizziness, and a child under 12 months with earache in both ears, are also on that list.

Pus or discharge from the ear, and symptoms of a middle ear infection that last more than 2 to 3 days, are listed as reasons to contact a clinician, and a GP appointment is the usual route. Swelling behind the ear, severe headache, dizziness or twitching of the face muscles are also listed as reasons to seek advice from NHS 111 or the GP the same day. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

faqs.q: Do ear infections go away on their own?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The NHS says ear infections usually settle without intervention and often improve within about 3 days. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease discomfort in the meantime. If symptoms last longer than 2 to 3 days, get worse, or fluid drains from the ear, contacting a GP or NHS 111 is the route to care.

Usually not. The NHS says antibiotics are not usually offered for middle ear infections because they make little difference to symptoms. NICE supports either no antibiotic or a back-up prescription for most children with acute otitis media. Immediate antibiotics are offered where a child is very unwell, has signs of a more serious illness or is at high risk of complications.

faqs.q: Is an ear infection the same as glue ear?
faqs.a: No. Glue ear is fluid building up in the middle ear, and one NHS leaflet notes it is not an ear infection. Fluid that stays after an infection can lead to it. It is common in young children and the hearing loss is usually mild or moderate.

The CDC advises receiving recommended vaccines, such as the flu and pneumococcal vaccines. Pneumococcal bacteria can cause ear infections. Secondhand smoke is described as a major cause of ear infections in children. Limiting exposure to tobacco smoke is described as a way to lower risk.

faqs.q: Can an ear infection affect hearing?
faqs.a: Most children have slight short-term hearing loss during and just after an ear infection, because of fluid in the ear. If fluid remains for weeks, it is called glue ear. New hearing loss is on the NHS list of reasons to contact a GP or NHS 111 urgently.
